Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection and dengue virus infection are common viral illnesses in tropical regions. However, concurrent infections are rarely reported and may present significant diagnostic challenges because of overlapping clinical manifestations, including fever, rash, and hematologic abnormalities.
We report a laboratory-confirmed co-infection with VZV and dengue virus in a previously healthy 17-year-old female patient from Quezon City, Philippines. She initially presented with a 3-day history of fever and a generalized pruritic vesicular rash and was treated for varicella with oral acyclovir. Despite antiviral therapy, persistent high-grade fever, epigastric abdominal pain, leukopenia (2.8 × 10⁹/l), and thrombocytopenia (85 × 10⁹/l) prompted further investigation on the fourth day of illness. Diagnostic testing confirmed acute dengue infection by positive nonstructural protein 1 antigen and dengue immunoglobulin M test results, while VZV polymerase chain reaction testing of vesicular fluid confirmed varicella. The patient received supportive dengue management alongside continued acyclovir therapy. Clinical symptoms improved, with resolution of fever by the sixth day of illness, normalization of hematologic parameters, and progressive crusting of lesions. She was discharged without complications.
This case highlights the importance of considering dengue co-infection in patients with apparent varicella who develop persistent fever, abdominal pain, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia in dengue-endemic settings. Early laboratory confirmation is essential to distinguish overlapping clinical features, guide appropriate management, and prevent missed or delayed diagnoses.

articles.titulo: Metabolite Screening Identifies Potent Antivirals that Mitigate Zika Virus-Induced Ocular Pathology.
articles.autores: Singh S, Jeyachandran AV, Daskou M, Zaiss A, Kolge H, Wright RE, Singhal A, Bonazzi A, Damoiseaux R, Arumugaswami V, Kumar A
articles.resumo_original: Zika virus (ZIKV) infection remains a significant global health threat due to its association with severe congenital, neurological, and ocular complications and the continued lack of approved antiviral therapies or vaccines. To identify new therapeutic candidates, we performed a high-throughput antiviral screen of 1,050 human endogenous and exosome-derived metabolites for their ability to attenuate ZIKV infection in human retinal pigment epithelial cells (RPE). This led to the identification of 10 metabolites that reduced ZIKV-induced cytopathic effects, which were further evaluated for antiviral activity and toxicity using physiologically relevant ocular infection models. Among these candidates, octanedioic acid, undecanedioic acid, and 10-undecen-1-ol emerged as the most effective, significantly reducing ZIKV replication and modulating innate immune responses in RPE cells. Analysis of host signaling revealed metabolite-associated changes in STAT1, AMPK, and YAP phosphorylation, identifying potential pathways tied to their antiviral activity. Importantly, in an immunocompetent mouse model of ZIKV-induced chorioretinal atrophy, treatment with these metabolites markedly reduced retinal lesions and immune cell infiltration, demonstrating in vivo therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings identify host-derived metabolites as promising antiviral candidates against ZIKV and warrant further translational investigation.

articles.titulo: Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses.
articles.autores: Odio CD, Aogo RA, Firdous S, Voirin C, Blanco-Rivera S, Lowman KE, Asante N, Broderson Y, Konda K, Hasund CM, Martinez-Perez A, Mpingabo PI, Law M, Jarvis C, Callier V, Hunsberger S, Abad Fernandez M, de Silva A, Kattappuram R, Bhushan G, Yek C, Manning J, Durbin AP, Cohen JI, Weiskopf D, Whitehead SS, Katzelnick LC
articles.resumo_original: Dengue is the canonical viral disease for which immune history is a determinant of protective versus pathogenic responses and immunogenicity. Yet, because of limitations in animal models and clinical presentation after peak viremia, how preinfection and early immune responses affect dengue outcome is not confirmed. We conducted a phase 1 clinical trial with 45 healthy adults to test whether secondary infection challenge with a heterotypic, full-length, attenuated virus increases viremia and immunogenicity compared with primary and tertiary infection. Viremia was associated with more, but still mild, clinical signs and symptoms, and secondary infection resulted in greater viremia, neutralizing antibodies, and protective T cell responses. However, those whose baseline antibodies most efficiently increased dengue virus replication in an in vitro assay experienced delayed inflammatory and adaptive immune activation, the highest viremia, strong acute immune responses, and waning of potent CD8+ T cells and antibodies. In contrast, higher baseline antibodies against the nonstructural protein 1 of multiple serotypes predicted early interferon and balanced immune activation, viremia control, and development of enduring, potent B and T cells, revealing how vaccines can induce broad, long-lasting protection. Last, individuals with potent and neutralizing antibodies and IFN-γ+ T cells at baseline experienced minimal viral replication. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled human challenge with dengue virus can delineate coordinated versus dysregulated acute immune responses and their effects on immunogenicity, informing therapeutic and vaccine strategies for dengue and other viral diseases.

articles.titulo: A Live Attenuated Dengue Virus Vaccine (Dengvaxia) is Suppressed in Individuals with Immunity to Serotype 4.
articles.autores: Adams C, Hein LD, White LJ, Shah R, Premkumar L, Daag JV, Agrupis KA, Crisostomo MV, Ylade M, Deen J, Lopez AL, de Silva AM
articles.resumo_original:
Dengvaxia® was the first live attenuated tetravalent dengue virus (DENV) vaccine to be tested and approved for use in people. While Dengvaxia was designed to be tetravalent, in humans, the vaccine performed like a monovalent DENV4 vaccine because the DENV4 vaccine virus replicated better than other vaccine serotypes. Dengvaxia® was safe and efficacious in children who were DENV-immune at baseline and contraindicated for use in DENV-naïve children.
When Dengvaxia® was rolled out as a pediatric vaccine in the Philippines in 2016, we established a prospective cohort to assess vaccine performance by baseline dengue serostatus. Here we report on how baseline monotypic immunity to each serotype (reflecting one past DENV infection) impacted Dengvaxia® responses.
We observed that in children with baseline immunity to DENV1, 2 or 3, the vaccine stimulated a secondary serotype cross-neutralizing Ab response, which likely explains the overall favorable performance of the vaccine in seropositive children enrolled in phase 3 trials. We observed a high frequency (61%) of vaccine suppression among DENV4 monotypic immune children.
Our results confirm the replication dominance of the DENV4 vaccine component in Dengvaxia® and directly implicate pre-existing DENV4 immunity in the suppression of the vaccine. Our results have broader implications for evaluating the performance of other DENV vaccines in seropositive individuals.

articles.titulo: mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in people with HIV: an immune correlates analysis of CD4 + T cell responses in the multicenter CoVPN 3008 observational study.
articles.autores: Khuzwayo S, Zhang B, Voillet V, Carpp LN, LaherOmar F, Peng J, Hu J, Schwedhelm K, Smit E, Magaret CA, Chen Z, Heng S, Jin Y, Elyanu PJ, Tapley A, Kee JJ, Hudson A, Bhebhe S, Kaldine H, Kgagudi P, Hermanus T, Andriesen J, Randhawa AK, Fisher LH, Villaran M, Polakowski L, Yacovone M, Samandari T, Chirenje Z, Badal-Faesen S, Brumskine W, Coetzer S, Dawson R, Delany-Moretlwe S, Diacon AH, Fry S, Gill KM, Hoosain ZAE, Hosseinipour MC, Inambao M, Innes C, Innes S, Kalonji D, Kasaro M, Kassim P, Kayange N, Kamuti E, Kilembe W, Laher F, Makhema J, Malahleha M, Maluleke VL, Mathebula M, Mboya G, McHarry K, Kityo Mutuluuza C, Mda P, Mitha E, Msomi S, Moloantoa T, Naicker N, Naicker V, Nanvubya A, Nuwagaba-Biribonwoha H, Otieno W, Potgieter EL, Potloane D, Punt Z, Said JA, Singh Y, Tayob MS, Vahed Y, Maena J, Cohen MS, Kublin JG, Gail Bekker L, Corey L, Gray GE, Huang Y, Mgodi NM, Dadabhai S, Kotze PL, Garrett N, Hural J, Ferrari G, Montefiori D, Moore PL, Tomaras GD, Mkhize NN, De Rosa SC, McElrath MJ, Gilbert PB, Andersen-Nissen E
articles.resumo_original: T cell correlates of COVID-19 risk are poorly defined, particularly in people with HIV (PWH). CoVPN 3008 ( NCT05168813 ) Part A was a prospective 14,002-participant cohort study that administered one or two doses of mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine, depending on baseline SARS-CoV-2 serostatus, in participants (83% PWH) in sub-Saharan Africa. Participants self-monitored for prespecified COVID-19 symptoms, defined by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention symptom criteria. Previous work showed that protection from COVID-19 was superior for hybrid versus vaccine-induced immunity, and that neutralizing antibody titers inversely associated with COVID-19 risk. In the present work, we measured T cell responses to Spike and Nucleocapsid at baseline and 4 weeks post last-vaccination (Peak) in a case-cohort study and assessed them as correlates of risk. In Hybrid Group PWH (n = 22 cases), COVID-19 risk over 6 months decreased with increasing Peak Spike BA.4/5-specific CD4 + T cell responses, from 15.8%, 4.7%, and 0% risk at 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% IFN-γ and/or IL-2 response magnitude, respectively. Including baseline Spike-specific neutralizing antibody titer and Peak CD4 + T cell functionality score in the same model increased the association's strength (overall p < 0.001). Thus, CD4 + T cell responses are an independent correlate of COVID-19 risk among PWH with pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity.

articles.titulo: Protein-Protein Interaction-Guided Peptides Interfere with Early Zika Virus Entry-Associated Events.
articles.autores: Rodríguez-Salazar CA, Recalde-Reyes DP, Linares-Jiménez S, López-Cardoso C, Giraldo MI
articles.resumo_original: Zika virus (ZIKV) remains a public health concern because of its association with neurological complications and congenital disease, yet no specific antiviral therapy has been approved. Since the envelope (E) protein mediates viral attachment and early entry-associated membrane events, it represents an attractive antiviral target. Here, we used a protein-protein interaction-guided strategy to design peptides to interfere with predicted interfaces between the ZIKV E protein and cellular receptors involved in attachment. After in silico filtering and preliminary screening, six peptides (PZ1-PZ6) were selected. These peptides showed heterogeneous physicochemical profiles, low cytotoxicity and hemolytic activity under the tested conditions, and docking-predicted interactions with functional E protein regions. In HTR-8/SVneo cells, antiviral activity depended on the timing of exposure, with greater reductions in infectious titers during co-treatment and post-treatment. All peptides also reduced titers in anti-adsorption assays, supporting interference with viral attachment or early entry-associated events. Consistently, DiOC18 fluorescence signals were reduced in a peptide-specific manner, particularly for PZ3 and PZ6. Nuclease protection assays showed no extensive exposure of the viral genome, whereas transmission electron microscopy revealed ultrastructural alterations without generalized particle disruption. Overall, PZ1-PZ6 are promising protein-protein interaction-guided anti-ZIKV peptide candidates with activity against early viral entry-associated events.

articles.titulo: Antiviral Sesquiterpene Lactones from Laurus nobilis L.: Inhibition of Hepatitis C Virus and Dengue Virus Replication.
articles.autores: Amen Y, Elsbaey M, Mpekoulis G, Christou E, Tsimpili H, Vassilaki N, Shimizu K, Zoidis G
articles.resumo_original: Natural products remain indispensable scaffolds in antiviral drug discovery, particularly against high-burden viral pathogens. In this study, two major sesquiterpene lactones, dehydrocostus lactone (1) and costunolide (2), were isolated from Laurus nobilis L. leaves and evaluated for their antiviral potential against hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). The structures of both compounds were confirmed by HRMS and 1D NMR spectroscopic analyses. In subgenomic replicon assays, the molecules inhibited HCV replication in the low-micromolar range (EC50=2.34 μM for 1 and 2.06 μM for 2) with favorable selectivity indices. In full-length HCV reporter systems, costunolide (2) displayed enhanced anti-HCV potency, reduced viral RNA and NS5A protein levels, and enhanced the suppressive effect of the clinically approved NS5A inhibitor, daclatasvir. Furthermore, costunolide (2) exhibited cross-flaviviridae activity, suppressing DENV replication (EC50=5.89 μM in replicon cells; EC50=1.27 μM post-infection in infectious virus assays), and demonstrated cooperative suppression of viral propagation along with reduced glutathione. Mechanistically, these results highlight the critical role of the sesquiterpene lactone core, and the observed enhanced combined activity between costunolide and reduced glutathione is consistent with a possible contribution of the NRF2/glutathione antioxidant axis to its anti-DENV action. Overall, this study highlights L. nobilis as a previously underexplored source of antiviral sesquiterpene lactones and establishes costunolide (2) as a promising lead against HCV and DENV, warranting further investigation across additional Flaviviridae members.

articles.titulo: From Asia to Africa: drivers of antimalarial drug resistance emergence and spread.
articles.autores: Serrato-Arroyo S, Segovia X, Huijben S
articles.resumo_original: Antimalarial drug resistance has repeatedly become established first in Southeast Asia and subsequently spread to sub-Saharan Africa, despite Africa bearing most of the global malaria burden. We evaluate eight hypotheses proposed to explain this pattern, spanning transmission intensity, parasite, host and vector biology, and treatment practices. We distinguish between the generation, establishment, expansion, and geographic spread of resistance, as these stages may be affected differently. The strongest evidence supports roles for transmission-dependent processes and earlier and more intense historical drug pressure. Parasite genetic background may also be important, while evidence for human genetics, recombination, vector-mediated effects, and poor-quality drugs is weaker. Overall, resistance emergence is likely shaped by multiple interacting pressures acting across parasite, vector, host, and health system scales.

articles.titulo: Factors associated with the optimal uptake of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine: The experiences of postpartum women attending child welfare clinics in three rural districts in the Western Region of Ghana.
articles.autores: Amugi G, Agudey DT, Gyimah NM, Mensah P, Kwarkye I, Yengliereh GYG, Claude KJ, Brookman-Eshun B, Chinbuah S
articles.resumo_original:
Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) is a key preventive strategy. However, optimal uptake remains inconsistent despite high antenatal care (ANC) attendance. This study assessed factors associated with optimal IPTp-SP uptake and explored the experiences of postpartum women in rural Ghana.
A convergent parallel mixed-method study was conducted among 1,155 postpartum women attending child welfare clinics in Jomoro, Prestea-Huni Valley and Ellembelle districts of the Western Region of Ghana. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires and analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Qualitative data from in-depth interviews and focus group discussions were analysed thematically to explore women's experiences and perceptions.
Among the 1,155 women enrolled, 812 (70.3%) took three or more doses of IPTp-SP (IPTp3-SP). Knowledge of malaria in pregnancy was high, with 92.7% correctly identifying its mode of transmission and 91.7% identifying ways of preventing malaria during pregnancy. Factors independently associated with IPTp3-SP included age 10-19 years compared with 20-29 years (aOR 2.17, 95% CI 1.21-3.88), gravidity of three compared with one (aOR 2.67, 95% CI: 1.58-4.50), and gravidity of four compared with one (aOR 1.83, 95% CI: 1.02-3.28). Lower odds were observed among uninsured women (aOR 0.36, 95% CI: 0.20-0.64), single women (aOR 0.64, 95% CI: 0.42-0.97), and cohabiting women (aOR 0.52, 95% CI: 0.34-0.79). ANC attendance showed a strong association with IPTp3-SP: women attending <4 ANC visits had lower odds of receiving IPTp3-SP than those attending 10 or more visits (aOR 0.08, 95% CI: 0.04-0.15). Nausea, dizziness, weakness, abdominal discomfort, vomiting and difficulty chewing the tablets affected their experiences and, for some women, willingness to continue treatment.
IPTp-SP uptake was relatively high. Predictors of optimal uptake include age, education, marital status, gravidity, health insurance status, and number of ANC visits. Women with fewer ANC visits were less likely to receive three or more doses. Reported side effects posed barriers to adherence. Strengthening ANC attendance and counselling on IPTp-SP expected side effects may improve completion of recommended doses.

articles.titulo: De novo assembly of complete Plasmodium falciparum isolate genomes using PacBio HiFi sequencing technology.
articles.autores: Nyarko PB, Quenu M, Guéry MA, Cohen C, Wagutu GK, Hamilton WL, Girgis ST, Makunin A, McCarthy SA, Lawniczak MKN, Claessens A
articles.resumo_original: Plasmodium falciparum possesses a highly structured genome with extensive sequence diversity concentrated in Variant Surface Antigen (VSA) families. These genes-var, rif, and stevor-play key roles in immune evasion and pathogenesis and are difficult to assemble using short-read sequencing technologies. Here, we applied PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing to generate high-quality de novo genome assemblies from 43 P. falciparum parasite cultures originating from community cases in The Gambia. Parasites were culture-adapted, cloned by limiting dilution where possible, and sequenced using high molecular weight DNA extracts. Assemblies from single-genotype lineages were constructed using hifiasm, producing complete chromosomal-length scaffolds with high base accuracy without requiring short-read polishing. We recovered full repertoires of var, rif, and stevor genes and classified them into known subgroups. Together, our results demonstrate that PacBio HiFi sequencing enables accurate assembly of complex P. falciparum genomes from natural infections. This work provides a valuable genomic resource for future studies of parasite evolution, transmission dynamics, and antigenic diversity, and suggests that VSA repertoires can serve as reliable proxies of genetic relatedness across infections.

articles.titulo: Synthesis, Characterization and Structural Elucidation of Biocompatible Hydroxychloroquine-Zinc Oxide Hybrid Nanoclusters as Synergistic Antiplasmodial Agents.
articles.autores: Rani S, Kumar B, Devi J, Manuja A
articles.resumo_original: Background: The increasing emergence of antimalarial drug resistance and safety concerns associated with conventional therapies necessitates the development of improved compounds. In this study, we report the synthesis of hydroxychloroquine-zinc oxide hybrid nanoclusters (HCQ-ZnONPs) by integrating a bioactive organic ligand (hydroxychloroquine) with a bioactive metal oxide nanocluster (ZnONPs). Methods: Structural and physicochemical characterization was performed using proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), mass spectrometry, X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX), dynamic light scattering (DLS), and zeta potential. Molecular docking against Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase-thymidylate synthase (PfDHFR-TS) was performed to investigate potential ligand-target interactions. Drug loading and HCQ release were evaluated at pH 7.4. We also assessed in vitro cytocompatibility, nitric oxide estimation, total antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory and antimalarial activities. Results: The physicochemical characterization supported the successful formation of HCQ-ZnONPs. In the proposed model of HCQ-ZnONPs, a quinoline nitrogen of the HCQ molecule interacts with an exposed Zn2+ site on the surface of a ZnONPs cluster. The HCQ-ZnONPs exhibited a drug loading of 21.4% and showed approximately 48.4% cumulative HCQ release over 24 h at pH 7.4. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of an HCQ-ZnONPs nanocluster system. Biological evaluation demonstrated synergistic in vitro antimalarial activity, indicating enhanced efficacy compared with the parent drug, suggesting that this arises from the integration of HCQ and ZnO nanoclusters while maintaining favorable cytocompatibility in Vero cells. The oxidative stress and anti-inflammatory potential of the hybrid complex was also assessed, highlighting its multifunctional biological profile that may be advantageous for mitigating malaria-associated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses. Molecular docking against PfDHFR-TSfurther supported favorable ligand-target interactions and provided additional insight into the potential molecular basis of the observed biological activity. Conclusions: Collectively, the experimental, theoretical, and mathematical analysis suggests the successful formation of HCQ-ZnONPs with promising anti-inflammatory and antimalarial efficacy, establishing this hybrid nano system as a potential candidate for next-generation antiplasmodial therapy.

articles.titulo: Harnessing omics to refine taxonomic classification in the malaria vector Anopheles gambiae species complex: a review.
articles.autores: Milugo TK, Kwi P, Ndiath MO, Assogba BS, Amambua-Ngwa A
articles.resumo_original: The malaria vector Anopheles gambiae s.l. (Diptera: Culicidae) is predominant in sub-Saharan Africa, where it plays a crucial role in transmitting malaria parasites to humans. Hitherto considered a single species, advances in cytogenetics and genomics have unveiled members of the complex as separate species. Whilst these species are morphologically indistinguishable, they are genetically distinct exhibiting significant differences in their ecological interactions and behavior. For example, they display considerable variation in their response to vector control measures and capacity to host malaria parasite, contributing differentially to malaria transmission. Consequently, precise taxonomic identification might help guide control programs against them. However, current approaches used in An. gambiae taxonomic systematics differ in accuracy and sensitivity, making it difficult to correctly delimit species boundaries. In this review, we discuss available taxonomic approaches utilized in An. gambiae complex whilst providing a framework for future taxonomic efforts. We also examine the process of naming a new species within the complex and detail the complexities of existing nomenclature approaches, as well as the prospective challenges they present, while advocating for an alternative approach. We conclude by providing a perspective on the use of a robust integrated approach in classifying and naming species of the An. gambiae complex.

articles.titulo: Insecticide resistance intensity in Anopheles gambiae s.l. populations from Nioro and Ndoffane health districts, Senegal.
articles.autores: Diallo S, Diop M, Faye MB, Diallo M, Touré A, Bodian G, Diagne NS, Tine EG, Diédhiou SM, Niang A, Konaté L, Dia I, Niang EHA
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains a major public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. In Senegal, the increasing resistance of Anopheles gambiae sensu lato (s.l.) to main public health insecticides threatens the effectiveness of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS). This study aimed to assess insecticide resistance intensity and to determine the distribution of kdr and Ace-1 resistance mutations in wild An. gambiae s.l. populations from Nioro and Ndoffane districts (Kaolack region).
Anopheles larvae were collected between September and November 2018 and reared under insectary conditions. Adult females were subjected to World Health Organization (WHO) susceptibility assays using five insecticides: three pyrethroids, one carbamate and one organophosphate. Resistance intensity assays were conducted at 5 × and 10 × diagnostic concentrations. Species within the An. gambiae complex and the East-kdr (1014S), West-kdr (1014F) and Ace-1 (G119S) were identified using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) technique.
A total of 1830 females An. gambiae s.l. were tested. Widespread resistance to pyrethroids and organophosphates was observed in both districts, while in Ndoffane complete susceptibility to bendiocarb was recorded and in Nioro resistance was observed. Anopheles arabiensis was the predominant species (> 90%), followed by An. gambiae s.s. and An. coluzzii. The frequencies of East-kdr and West-kdr mutations were higher in Ndoffane (40.4% and 30.8%) than in Nioro (10.6% and 13.1%). The Ace-1 (G119S) mutation was detected exclusively in the heterozygous state across all the study populations.
The studied vectors exhibit multiple insecticide resistance mechanisms, likely driven by combined selection pressures from agricultural and public health insecticide use. Strengthening entomological surveillance and implementing integrated resistance management strategies are essential to preserve the effectiveness of malaria vector control interventions in Senegal.

articles.titulo: Epidemiology of malaria and district-level factors associated with malaria elimination in Sumatra region, Indonesia: a retrospective analysis of surveillance data.
articles.autores: Lestari KD, Surendra H, Djaafara BA, Fadilah I, Ekawati LL, Susanto H, Prameswari HD, Fajariyani SB, Supriyanto D, Herdiana H, Conway E, Charoen P, Lawpoolsri S, Pan-Ngum W, Elyazar IRF
articles.resumo_original:
As transmission declines, malaria becomes more spatially and demographically concentrated. This study investigated individual-level malaria characteristics and district-level factors associated with elimination in all 154 districts in Sumatra, Indonesia.
We analysed individual-level data of 13,386 reported malaria cases from 2019 to 2021. P. falciparum and P. vivax were confirmed by microscopy or rapid diagnostic test, while probable P. knowlesi was defined as microscopically identified P. knowlesi. Cases were classified as imported if they reported travel to endemic region within 2-4 weeks. Multivariable logistic regression with province as a random effect was used to examine individual-level factors associated with imported cases, and district-level socioeconomic and environmental factors associated with elimination. Spatial clustering of indigenous cases was assessed using Global Moran's I and SaTScan.
Among reported cases, 71.8% (9,617) were P. vivax, 18.4% (2,467) P. falciparum, and 2.8% (369) probable P. knowlesi. Of 11,390 investigated cases, 8,748 (76.8%) were indigenous, 1,741 (15.3%) imported, and 901 (7.9%) unclassified. Imported cases were associated with older age (adjusted odds ratio 1.79, 95%CI 1.42-2.25 for 15-24 years old, and 1.97, 1.59-2.46 for 25-64 years old, compared to < 15 years old), males (1.70, 1.43-2.03), mobile and migrant population-related occupations (1.46, 1.22-1.76), diagnosed at hospitals or clinics (2.32, 1.85-2.91), infected with P. falciparum (1.48, 1.22-1.80), and hospitalised (15.29, 12.66-18.46). At the district level, a higher human development index (1.15, 1.01-1.34), lower historical annual parasite incidence (0.46, 0.29-0.69), and fewer endemic neighbours (0.78, 0.67-0.89) were associated with a higher likelihood of elimination. Spatial analysis revealed clustering tendencies, with localised clusters for P. falciparum, P. vivax, and probable P. knowlesi.
Dynamics of imported malaria, heterogeneous clusters of local transmission, and lower district-level human development index challenged elimination efforts. This highlights the need for strengthened surveillance and targeted interventions.

articles.titulo: Spatiotemporally coordinated immunometabolic-hyperthermia therapy for diabetic bone defect regeneration.
articles.autores: Wang L, Peng X, Zheng L, Liu Y, Chen L, Li X, Wang Z
articles.resumo_original: Diabetic bone defects (DBDs) are typified by persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, and microbial infection within the diabetic microenvironment, which collectively hinder osteogenesis and angiogenesis. Herein, we introduce an Immunometabolic-Hyperthermia Therapy (IMHT) strategy based on a dual-functional nanoplatform, namely a polydopamine/itaconate-incorporated agarose/gelatin (PIAG) hydrogel. This system is fabricated by incorporating itaconic acid (ITA) into polydopamine (PDA) nanoparticles through in situ polymerization, followed by encapsulation within a gelatin/agarose matrix. ITA primarily provides immunometabolic regulation, while PDA enables a tunable photothermal response. Upon localized photothermal heating (∼50 °C), the PIAG hydrogel effectively disrupts bacterial biofilms, with photothermal treatment providing the dominant antibacterial effect and ITA offering an additional supportive contribution. Upon mild photothermal activation (∼41 °C), IMHT mitigates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, inhibits neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and reprograms macrophages toward an M2-like reparative phenotype through JAK1/STAT1 pathway inhibition. The resulting pro-regenerative immune milieu enhances fibroblast growth factor-2 (FGF-2) secretion, while heat-induced activation of HSP90 stabilizes FGF-2/FGFR1 signaling, further promoting osteogenic differentiation and endothelial migration. Overall, the spatiotemporally coordinated antibacterial, immunometabolic, and regenerative regulation realized by IMHT offers a comprehensive and effective strategy for the repair of diabetic bone defects.

articles.titulo: From expression profiling to functional validation: evidence hierarchy and biomarker readiness of circular RNAs in aquatic animals.
articles.autores: Song KS, Guo M, Li CH
articles.resumo_original: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed non-coding RNA molecules that are mainly generated from precursor mRNAs through back-splicing. Owing to the lack of free 5' and 3' ends, circRNAs exhibit high stability and pronounced spatiotemporal expression specificity. In aquatic animals, recent advances in high-throughput sequencing and bioinformatic analysis have greatly expanded the catalog of circRNAs and uncovered their regulatory roles in growth, gonadal development, tissue regeneration, immune defense, and environmental stress responses. This review provides a systematic overview of circRNA biogenesis, representative molecular functions, identification strategies, and bioinformatic resources in aquatic animals, with particular emphasis on circRNA-mediated regulation during bacterial and viral infection, antiparasitic defense, trained immunity, and responses to physicochemical stressors. We further summarize the current evidence supporting the potential of circRNAs as candidate biomarkers for economically important traits, infectious disease monitoring, and ecotoxicological assessment. Importantly, we highlight the major bottlenecks that currently limit progress in this field, including incomplete genome annotation, algorithm-dependent identification bias, and the lack of robust in vivo functional validation. Overall, aquatic animals provide valuable non-model systems for expanding our understanding of circRNA biology, although many proposed regulatory mechanisms and translational applications remain to be further validated.

articles.titulo: A voltage-gated porin PPE1 regulates secretion and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
articles.revista: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
articles.autores: Yadav M, C A NF, Mandal D, Shukla J, Sarkar B, Kumar Mahtha S, Chandramouli A, Prasad A, Kamat SS, Mohanty D, Dutta S, Mahendran KR, Gokhale RS
articles.resumo_original: Drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a formidable clinical hurdle, compounded by the fact that the pathways by which antibiotics penetrate its multilayered cell envelope remain incompletely mapped. We identify PPE1 as a voltage-gated outer-membrane porin that mediates the secretion of kupyaphores while also facilitating the uptake of the frontline anti-tubercular drug isoniazid (INH). Genome-wide association analysis of 38,038 clinical isolates links ppe1 mutations with INH resistance, highlighting its clinical relevance. Consistent with this, the Mtb Δppe1 mutant shows increased tolerance to INH, accompanied by markedly reduced intracellular accumulation of INH compared with the wild-type strain. The Δppe1 strain exhibits attenuated infection, impaired growth, and reduced virulence in a murine infection model. Electron microscopy, molecular modeling, and single-channel electrophysiology reveal that PPE1 assembles into an unusual pentameric α-helical channel, distinct from classical β-barrel bacterial porins. Together, our findings identify PPE1 as a key determinant of mycobacterial membrane permeability that coordinates metallophore secretion and also antibiotic influx. This work uncovers a previously unrecognized mechanism governing Mtb physiology, virulence, and drug susceptibility, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

articles.titulo: Ginsenoside Rd alleviates atherosclerosis by inhibiting adipocyte ferroptosis in perivascular adipose tissues.
articles.autores: Fu X, Liu C, Hu F, Qin J, Wang T, Li X
articles.resumo_original:
Ginsenoside Rd (Rd) is an active ingredient in Panax ginseng Meyer and can be absorbed into the adipose tissue. Here, we aimed to investigate the impact of Rd on atherosclerosis (AS) and explore the mechanism.
We constructed an AS model by feeding ApoE-/- mice with a standard Western high-fat diet, treated with Rd, and combined RORC and TIGAR adipocyte-specific adeno-associated virus infection. An inflammatory adipocyte model (3T3-L1) was induced by LPS, and a lipid accumulation model in adipocytes was induced by palmitic acid. We investigated the role of the Rd-mediated RORC/TIGAR axis in adipocyte inflammation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis through lentiviral vectors and the ferroptosis activator erastin. The interactions between RORC and TIGAR were examined. Next, the degree of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis within perivascular adipose tissues (PVAT) in mice and 3T3-L1 cells was assessed.
Rd improved PVAT dysfunction and alleviated endothelial inflammation in AS mice. Rd targeted and inhibited RORC expression in adipocytes within the PVAT of mice. The transcription factor RORC occupied the TIGAR promoter to repress TIGAR transcription. Reactivation of RORC reversed the therapeutic benefit of Rd on AS, and reactivation of TIGAR also alleviated AS exacerbated by RORC. Rd reached therapeutic benefits by inhibiting RORC expression in adipocytes within PVAT, weakening its inhibitory effect on TIGAR, and further inhibiting adipocyte ferroptosis.
Rd targets RORC to activate TIGAR expression and block adipocyte ferroptosis in PVAT, thereby inhibiting AS.

articles.titulo: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates TH17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis.
articles.autores: Zhang C, Liu X, Xu N, Chen H, Gao Y, Gu C, Shen X, Wu J, Lu X, Zhang P, He Y, Xu Z, Su W
articles.resumo_original: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (TH17) cell-mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and multilayered metabolomic profiling in patients with AU and experimental AU models, we identified the lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor GPR183 as a key immunometabolic regulator in pathogenic CD4+ T cells. Upon activation, GPR183 modulates intracellular signaling via suppression of cyclic adenosine monophosphate-cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity and promotion of son-of-sevenless-dependent KRAS activation, which in turn elicits copper overload-induced mitochondrial oxidative stress, structural impairment, and metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis, thereby promoting TH17 cell pathogenicity. For clinical translation, virtual screening of Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs coupled with molecular docking and microscale thermophoresis validation identified fluvoxamine (FLV) as a direct GPR183 antagonist. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic TH17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. These findings delineate a unique GPR183-KRAS-mitochondrial damage axis governing TH17-driven autoimmunity and support repurposing FLV as a translatable therapeutic approach for AU and other autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

articles.titulo: Synthetic auxotrophy reveals metabolic regulation of plasma cell generation, affinity maturation, and cytokine receptor signaling.
articles.autores: Cho SH, Brookens SK, Raybuck AL, Meyer K, Paik Y, Hamilton J, Li J, Kalecky K, Park C, Lim J, Hicks SL, Karijolich J, Bottiglieri TH, Rathmell JC, Mogilenko D, Scharer CD, Boothby MR
articles.resumo_original: The proliferation and development of activated B lymphocytes into antibody (Ab)-secreting plasma cells are critical determinants of humoral immunity and sustain certain autoimmune diseases. Specific pathways and substrate supplies in intermediary metabolism influence lymphocyte differentiation and function. We now show that although stringent restriction of glutamine supply decreases B cell proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells, glutaminolysis - a major metabolic use of this amino acid - was only conditionally crucial in B cells and the Ab responses derived from them. Gls, the gene encoding the main glutaminase of lymphocytes, promoted anti-NP Ab responses at the primary and recall phases if either glucose uptake into mouse B cells or pyruvate into their mitochondria was also impaired. Otherwise, it was dispensable. This synthetic auxotrophy, that is, the conditional requirement of glutaminase for processes in addition to survival, involved supporting progressive expansion of mitochondrial respiration followed by plasma cell differentiation. Surprisingly, impairment of glutaminase and the mitochondrial pyruvate channel decreased IL-21 stimulation of STAT3 phosphorylation as well as interferon stimulation of STAT1 activation. Together, our findings establish a powerful collaboration of metabolic pathways in programming increased respiration and the development of Ab-secreting cells, but also reveal modulation of cytokine receptor signaling by metabolism.

articles.titulo: Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study.
articles.autores: Witowski A, Bracht T, Kröger L, Rump K, Nowak H, Bergmann L, Unterberg M, Rahmel T, Westhus B, Wolf A, Thon P, Ziehe D, Putensen C, Ehrentraut S, Zarbock A, Wappler F, Defosse J, Henzler D, Sitek B, Schnitzbauer A, Stervbo U, Rosiewicz K, Hugo C, Neumann S, Pagel P, Pascher A, Babel N, Adamzik M, Dyck B, Koos B
articles.resumo_original:
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID).
SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles.
In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

articles.titulo: Functional consequences of acanthocephalan infection in Homarus americanus and advances in understanding of parasite-associated changes in lobster immunity.
articles.autores: Ghiasvand Z, MacCormack TJ, Rampaul M, Pickett S, Clark KF
articles.resumo_original: Profilicollis botulus is an acanthocephalan parasite with larval stages developing in arthropod intermediate hosts and adult stages maturing in vertebrate definitive hosts, typically seabirds. Despite its widespread occurrence in coastal ecosystems, the physiological and molecular consequences of P. botulus infection in the American lobster (Homarus americanus) remain unclear. In this exploratory observational study, we combined whole-animal respirometry with hepatopancreas RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to characterize physiological and transcriptional differences between naturally infected and uninfected lobsters. Infected lobsters exhibited significantly lower mass-specific oxygen consumption than uninfected individuals (28.51 ± 1.87 vs 35.02 ± 1.49 mg O₂ kg-1 h-1). Exploratory transcriptomic analysis of a limited number of individuals (four infected and three uninfected) identified 324 differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05), including 232 downregulated and 92 upregulated transcripts in infected lobsters. Several transcripts associated with glycolysis and related metabolic processes showed higher expression in infected individuals. Conversely, lower transcript abundance was observed for multiple genes associated with innate immune functions, including lectin-type pattern recognition receptors, antimicrobial peptides (including anti-lipopolysaccharide factors), and components of the prophenoloxidase and coagulation systems, antioxidant enzymes, acute-phase proteins, and crustacean hyperglycemic hormone. Together, these findings associate reduced aerobic metabolism with lower expression of multiple innate immune-related transcripts in the hepatopancreas, a pattern that may be compatible with a stabilized host-parasite interaction and altered energetic allocation during parasitism. However, given the observational design and limited transcriptomic sample size, these interpretations remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms. Together with other studies of parasite infections in crustaceans, our findings suggest that host responses to acanthocephalan infection may be host-dependent and influenced by parasite biology, tissue specificity, and host physiological condition. Further studies incorporating larger sample sizes, controlled infection experiments, and functional measurements are needed to determine whether these associations reflect direct effects of infection or other host-related and environmental factors.

articles.titulo: NLRP3 inflammasome dysregulation in chronic bacterial infections: mechanistic insights into treatment failure and relapse.
articles.autores: Girdhar J, Jangra S, Rastogi A, Saxena R
articles.resumo_original: Chronic and recurrent bacterial infections are a significant clinical issue despite the development of antimicrobial treatment. It is increasingly being shown that chronic host-based inflammatory dysregulation is also an integral cause of treatment failure and persistence of illness, and not just the consequence of microbial resistance. The NLRP3 inflammasome presents an important integrated platform linking tissue destruction, metabolic strain, and microbial detection to augmented inflammatory reactions. The ultimate goal of the review is to assess chronic bacterial infection as an inflammatory resolution dysfunction, and the example of persistent NLRP3 inflammasome dysregulation and the therapeutic consequences. In this review, the existing data on the canonical and non-canonical pathways of NLRP3 activation is summarized and the interplay between metabolic reprogramming, ionic flux, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired autophagy are all thought to contribute to the lowered activation thresholds in chronic infection. The disease-specific pathology of the prolonged IL-1β and IL-18 generation, destabilisation of the barricade and inflammatory feedback prolongation are common pathological themes in contexts like granulomatous lung disease, intracellular persistence syndromes, biofilm-associated infections and chronic airway colonisation. Inflammasome permissiveness and resolution are exacerbated by immunometabolic changes and microbiome imbalance.

articles.titulo: Dietary Fiber Improves High-Fat Diet-Induced Hyperglycemia by Modulating Intestinal ILC3-Mediated Immunity through the SCFA-FFAR2 Pathway.
articles.revista: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.autores: Mou Y, Long F, Qi C, Huang W, Du Q, Zhang Y, Yu C, Zhou J
articles.resumo_original: Dietary fiber intake is associated with improved glycemic control in high-fat diet-induced hyperglycemia, yet the immunological mechanisms linking gut microbiota-derived metabolites to host defense remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated whether dietary fiber ameliorates these metabolic disorders by modulating intestinal group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) via short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and their receptor FFAR2. In a 12-week fiber-supplemented high-fat diet mouse model, fiber alleviated hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and intestinal barrier dysfunction. Mechanistically, fiber increased cecal SCFAs (especially propionate), which activated colonic ILC3s in an FFAR2-dependent manner. FFAR2 triggered ERK and STAT3 phosphorylation and directly bound STAT3 to facilitate its phosphorylation, boosting IL-22 transcription. SCFA-activated ILC3s strengthened epithelial barrier integrity via elevated tight-junction proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that dietary fiber restores gut barrier function through the SCFA-FFAR2-ERK/STAT3-IL-22 axis in ILC 3s, highlighting ILC3-expressed FFAR2 as a potential therapeutic target for high-fat diet-related metabolic disorders.

articles.titulo: Powerhouses of lethality: mitochondria in macrophage antimicrobial activity.
articles.autores: McFadden MJ, O'Meara TR, O'Riordan MX
articles.resumo_original: Macrophages employ multiple strategies to dispatch phagocytosed microbes, including bombardment with toxic compounds and radicals, or the deprivation of key nutrients. The lethality of macrophages depends on their ability to regulate levels of microbicidal effectors and proper targeting of these effectors to the phagosome, where many intracellular pathogens are detained. Mitochondria play important roles in establishing an antimicrobial phagosomal environment in macrophages, playing roles in both the production and targeting of these effectors. In response to infection, the mitochondrial network undergoes dramatic structural and functional perturbations that modulate macrophage microbicidal potential. As central coordinators of cellular metabolism, mitochondria control the abundance of metabolites that can either be toxic to ingested microbes or necessary for their growth. Mitochondria are also prolific producers of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which play direct roles in killing microbes and serve as signaling molecules to coordinate antimicrobial responses. While mitochondria are also known to play extensive roles in regulating cytokine production and proinflammatory responses, this review will focus on highlighting mechanisms by which mitochondria manipulate the macrophage microbicidal milieu.

articles.titulo: [LGALS3 is an efferocytosis-related biomarker and potential traditional Chinese medicine therapeutic target for diabetic kidney disease complicated with heart failure].
articles.revista: Nan fang yi ke da xue xue bao = Journal of Southern Medical University
articles.autores: Hu D, Guo H, Wang X, Li Y, Zhang C, Chen X, Nie X
articles.resumo_original:
To explore the immune efferocytosis mechanisms of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) complicated with chronic heart failure (CHF) in light of the glucose heart kidney axis and predict the "same treatment for different diseases" strategy using traditional Chinese medicine (TCM).
DKD and CHF transcriptome data from public databases were integrated to construct a core gene set using differential expression and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). The hub genes were intersected with an efferocytosis-related gene set, validated with external datasets, and functionally enriched. The Coremine Medical database and molecular docking were used to predict the regulatory TCMs, their properties, and affinities between the active ingredients and their targets. Clinical serum samples were collected form patients with DKD, CHF, and DKD+CHF and healthy individuals for detecting galectin 3 (LGALS3) levels.
Fifty comorbidity core genes were identified, which were enriched mainly in the PI3K Akt, TNF, AGE RAGE, and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. LGALS3 was identified as a key efferocytosis-associated hub gene with differential expression in the validation set. The prediction results included 216 TCMs predominantly exhibiting cold or warm properties with bitter, sweet or pungent flavors and liver, lung, spleen and kidney meridian tropisms. Molecular docking suggested strong binding between the key ingredients (e.g., quercetin) and LGALS3. Serum LGALS3 levels were significantly higher in patients with DKD+CHF than in those with DKD or CHF alone or healthy controls (all P<0.001). After adjusting for covariates, comorbid status remained independently and positively associated with LGALS3 (β=51.20, P<0.001), exceeding the independent contribution of NT proBNP.
DKD-CHF is associated with inflammatory/metabolic abnormalities and impairment of efferocytosis-mediated immune clearance. LGALS3 is a critical node connecting inflammatory pathways to target organ efferocytosis dysfunction. The predicted TCMs highlight the TCM therapeutic principles of "supplementing Qi, clearing the heat and resolving stasis" and may regulate efferocytosis and the immunometabolic microenvironment by targeting LGALS3.

articles.titulo: Beyond Targeted Delivery: The Emerging Immunomodulatory Landscape of Antibody-Oligonucleotide Conjugates.
articles.autores: Wang Y, Wang S, Wang H
articles.resumo_original: Antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) are usually viewed as delivery vehicles that carry nucleic-acid payloads to defined cell populations for gene silencing or gene regulation. Existing reviews concentrate on delivery systems, tumour-directed therapy and extrahepatic oligonucleotide delivery, while the intrinsic immunomodulatory activity of AOCs has received far less attention. Conjugation couples antibody-mediated targeting with the innate immune-stimulating activity of the payload, a property that most current AOCs seldom exploit. This review repositions AOCs as active immune regulators. Three emerging immunoregulatory applications are examined in detail: vaccine-adjuvant construction, neutrophil-driven innate immune activation, and immunometabolic reprogramming. Structure-activity relationships linking AOC design to immune potency are summarized, and their immune mechanisms are distinguished from those of free oligonucleotides and unconjugated antibodies. Based on preclinical and in vitro evidence, AOCs act as multifunctional immunomodulators rather than passive cargo carriers. Two sources of immune activity are distinguished: direct immunostimulation by the conjugated payload, and effects secondary to targeted delivery. These findings still await clinical confirmation. Key barriers to translation, including conjugation efficiency, mechanistic gaps and manufacturing bottlenecks, are discussed. Prospective applications include engineered vaccines, anti-infective innate therapy, tumour microenvironment remodelling and autoimmune intervention, pending further validation. This review provides a conceptual framework for developing next-generation AOC-based immune adjuvants and precision immunotherapeutics.

articles.titulo: Beyond Neuroinflammation: Targeting the Microbe-Barrier-Brain Axis Through Precision Nutrition in Neurological Long COVID (Neuro-PASC).
articles.autores: Velázquez De Castro-Bono A, Castro-Luna G, Guil-Guerrero JL
articles.resumo_original: Post-acute Neurological Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Neuro-PASC) contribute substantially to Long COVID-related disability, with cognitive impairment, chronic fatigue, dysautonomia, and neuropsychiatric symptoms among its most debilitating manifestations. Although its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, evidence implicates persistent immune activation, intestinal barrier dysfunction, microbiota dysbiosis, microbiome-derived metabolic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroimmune interactions in sustaining neuroinflammation and neurological impairment. This narrative review examines precision nutrition as a potential pathway-oriented strategy for Neuro-PASC. We synthesise evidence linking the gut microbiota, intestinal permeability, immunometabolic pathways, mitochondrial function, and neurological outcomes, while evaluating nutritional interventions targeting these mechanisms. We focus on candidate biomarkers, including serum zonulin, fatty acid-binding protein 2 (FABP2), faecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, which may support patient stratification and personalised nutritional strategies. We also propose a stepwise framework involving dietary stabilisation, functional foods, targeted supplementation, and microbiome-based interventions, alongside practical considerations for post-exertional symptom exacerbation, dysautonomia, and mast cell-related symptoms. Finally, we identify priorities for future research, including multi-omics integration, artificial intelligence, digital health, and biomarker-stratified randomised controlled trials. Because current evidence remains predominantly observational and mechanistic, precision nutrition should be considered a complementary strategy requiring rigorous clinical validation.

articles.titulo: c-Myc Links TGF-β Signaling to Metabolic Control of HIV Reactivation in OM10.1 Cells.
articles.autores: Harrison-Gleason J, Kim J, Martinelli E
articles.resumo_original: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV replication but does not eliminate persistent viral reservoirs, which can rapidly reseed viremia following treatment interruption. We previously showed that blockade of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signaling in vivo promotes SIV latency reversal and is associated with reversal of cellular metabolic quiescence. Here, using the provirally infected promyelocytic OM10.1 cell line, we investigated the cell-intrinsic mechanisms through which TGF-β regulates HIV reactivation. TGF-β inhibited proviral reactivation following stimulation with distinct latency-reversing agents, and this effect was reversed by pharmacologic inhibition of TGF-β signaling. TGF-β reduced HIV transcription without suppressing TNF-α-induced NF-κB activation, suggesting inhibition through an alternative mechanism. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed broad suppression of c-Myc-associated pathways, oxidative phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signaling. Functional metabolic profiling confirmed marked reductions in both glycolytic and mitochondrial ATP production and decreased mitochondrial membrane polarization. Consistent with a functional link between metabolism and viral reactivation, mitochondrial uncoupling strongly inhibited HIV expression. Finally, MYC overexpression completely rescued HIV transcription and partially restored p24 production in TGF-β-treated cells. Together, these findings identify a cell-intrinsic mechanism through which TGF-β restrains HIV reactivation by imposing a metabolically quiescent state, mediated at least in part through suppression of c-Myc.

articles.titulo: Lactate-Driven Biphasic Reprogramming of Macrophage Immune Responses.
articles.autores: Guo Q, Ren P, He L, Gao J, Lu R, Wang Y, Zhang Z, Han X, Zhang X, Fang C
articles.resumo_original: Lactate is a metabolic substrate, an extracellular signaling molecule, and a precursor for protein lactylation, with diverse effects on macrophage immunity. Evidence from infection, tissue injury, efferocytosis, and cancer indicates that lactate-associated pathways can amplify inflammation, support resolution and tissue repair, or sustain immune suppression. These outcomes depend on the timing, cellular source and compartment, chemical formulation and pH, transport and receptor engagement, and the chemistry and targets of lactylation. In this narrative review, we critically synthesize the biochemical foundations of lactate metabolism and lactyl-group donation and examine the mechanisms underlying these distinct macrophage responses. We distinguish model-specific biphasic responses from a universal sequence of early inflammation followed by resolution, and separate reparative programs from impaired antimicrobial or antitumor immunity. We also evaluate evidence for histone and non-histone lactylation, emphasizing the limits of metabolic perturbations and chromatin associations for establishing site-specific causality. This framework identifies experimental variables that should be controlled and supports context-selective investigation of lactate-related therapeutic targets in inflammatory diseases and cancer.

articles.titulo: New strategies for the treatment of tuberculosis: research progress and clinical translation in immune modulation and inflammation control.
articles.autores: Du S, Zhen L, Zhou J, Deng D
articles.resumo_original: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health challenge, with treatment complicated by drug resistance, adverse effects, and suboptimal host immune responses. Whilst conventional anti-TB drugs are effective bactericidally, their immunomodulatory effects may, in certain contexts, contribute to immune imbalance and affect treatment outcomes. Host-directed therapy (HDT), which aims to modulate the host immune response to enhance pathogen control and limit immunopathology, has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy. This narrative review critically evaluates the current evidence for HDT in TB, focusing on immunosenescence, trained immunity, cytokine and lipid mediator networks, immunometabolic reprogramming, neuroendocrine regulation, and repurposed drugs including metformin and statins. Importantly, we distinguish between evidence derived directly from TB models (in vitro, animal, and clinical studies) and evidence extrapolated from other diseases, highlighting knowledge gaps and areas requiring further investigation. We propose that future progress depends on evidence-based stratification of HDT candidates, rigorous clinical trial design, and a personalised approach that accounts for patient comorbidities and immune status. This review aims to provide a balanced framework for advancing HDT from bench to bedside in TB therapy.

articles.titulo: VZV reactivation, immune remodeling, and dementia risk.
articles.autores: Zhang L, Wu S, Quan Y, Yao W
articles.resumo_original: Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) is a highly dermatotropic and neurotropic α-herpesvirus that causes varicella (chickenpox) during primary infection, subsequently establishing lifelong latency, and reactivates to cause herpes zoster when host immunity declines or suppressed. Recent large-scale epidemiological studies consistently associate herpes zoster immunization, particularly with the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), with a significantly reduced risk of incident dementia. These findings have prompted a rigorous re-evaluation of the infectious etiology of progressive neurodegeneration. This review integrates the intersecting molecular mechanisms of VZV latency, localized ganglionic immunosenescence, and systemic inflammaging. We critically evaluate a synergistic VZV-HSV-1 amyloidogenic cascade, while explicitly addressing the biological limitations of extrapolating these transient interactions to human central nervous system (CNS) neuropathology. Furthermore, we propose the hypothesis that AS01B-induced trained immunity may contribute to neuroprotection. Therefore, this review provides insight for understanding the systemic consequences of chronic VZV infection and the impact of adjuvant-mediated immune remodeling in aging populations.

articles.titulo: Single-cell transcriptomics uncovers persistent hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection in obese hosts.
articles.autores: Qian W, Wei X, Park SJ, Garcia Diaz J, Comlekoglu T, Yu J, Sun J, Hahn YS
articles.resumo_original: SARS-CoV-2 infection affects multiple organs, and chronic post-viral tissue injury is often associated with persistent immune dysregulation. Obesity and related metabolic disorders are major risk factors for severe COVID-19 and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), including liver dysfunction. To define hepatic responses during post-acute infection, we studied lean and diet-induced obese mice at 7 and 28 days following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2. Compared with lean mice, obese mice exhibited persistent lung inflammation and fibrosis, along with liver injury characterized by increased lipid accumulation, cellular apoptosis, and metabolic dysfunction. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed obesity-associated alterations in hepatic immune and metabolic programs during post-acute infection. In particular, hepatic macrophages in obese mice showed sustained inflammatory and metabolic transcriptional alterations, while hepatocytes displayed altered programs associated with gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism. Endothelial cells also exhibited persistent transcriptional changes linked to immune activation and prothrombotic pathways. These alterations remained evident at 28 days post-infection, suggesting incomplete restoration of immune and metabolic homeostasis in obese liver. Collectively, our findings reveal persistent obesity-associated hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection and identify cellular and molecular programs that may contribute to post-acute liver sequelae in metabolically compromised hosts.

articles.titulo: Dietary Vitamin Intake and Cognitive Performance in Adults with Long COVID: The BioICOPER Study.
articles.autores: Arjol D, Arroyo-Romero S, García DR, Navarro-Matías E, Navarro-Cáceres A, Suárez-Moreno N, Domínguez-Martín A, Gómez-Marcos MA, Gómez-Sánchez M, Gómez-Sánchez L, BioICOPER Investigators Group
articles.resumo_original: Background: Long COVID (LC) is associated with persistent cognitive symptoms, frequently described as brain fog, and with inflammatory, immunometabolic, and energetic mechanisms potentially involved in cognitive functioning. Vitamins participate in biological processes relevant to brain function, but the relationship between habitual dietary vitamin intake and cognitive performance in LC remains poorly studied. Objective: To analyze the relationship between dietary vitamin intake and cognitive performance in adults with LC, considering both objective performance and self-reported cognition. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 304 adults with LC. Vitamin intake from foods and beverages was estimated using the EVIDENT seven-day dietary record, previously compared with a validated food-frequency questionnaire. Objective cognitive performance was assessed using normative scores from the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and the Memory Index Score (MIS), as well as MoCA domains and items. Self-reported cognition was assessed using the 30-item Memory Failures of Everyday Questionnaire (MFE-30) and the cognitive subscale of the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS). Primary global associations were examined using multiple linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors, whereas bounded MoCA domains were analyzed using proportional-odds ordinal regression and binary item-level outcomes using logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied within prespecified families of contrasts. Results: No associations between vitamin intake and global normative cognitive performance remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Median MoCA and MIS scores were 24.00 (IQR, 21.00-26.00) and 11.00 (IQR, 9.00-13.00), respectively. Normative MoCA and MIS scores showed medians of -0.32 (IQR, -0.82 to 0.19) and -0.32 (IQR, -0.76 to 0.14), respectively. Most participants (95.1%) met the dietary reference value for vitamin B3. In secondary ordinal analyses, higher vitamin B3 intake was associated with better MoCA language performance in the fully adjusted model (OR per 1 SD = 2.18, 95% CI 1.45-3.27, p < 0.001, q = 0.0116). No associations remained significant after FDR correction for everyday cognitive complaints, cognitive fatigue, or MoCA Memory and MoCA Multiple scores. Conclusions: In adults with LC, the primary analyses did not identify FDR-significant associations between habitual dietary vitamin intake and global normative cognitive performance. The secondary vitamin B3-language association requires independent confirmation and does not establish a cognitive benefit of higher intake or supplementation. These findings require confirmation in longitudinal studies incorporating nutritional biomarkers, information on supplementation, and broader neuropsychological assessment.

articles.titulo: Immunometabolic reprogramming of macrophages and neutrophils in acute pancreatitis: from metabolic stress to amplification and endogenous braking.
articles.autores: Ai Y, Zhang L, Wei A, Dong J, Pang T, Zhang Y, Wu K, Yao S
articles.resumo_original: Acute pancreatitis (AP) progression involves both the initiating acinar injury and immune responses that sustain or contain subsequent damage. This review integrates evidence on metabolic regulation in macrophages and neutrophils to examine its links to inflammatory effectors, clearance, and tissue protection. Glycolytic regulation can support inflammatory activation, while non-AP neutrophil studies show how substrate allocation supports oxidant production and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) release. Metabolite signaling also participates in macrophage efferocytosis, repair-associated responses, and tissue antioxidant defense. Contrasting lactate effects in acinar injury and macrophage repair indicate that metabolic changes must be interpreted through their effects on particular cells and functions. We propose an integrated amplification-braking framework that connects metabolically supported inflammatory effectors to continued generation of injury-derived stimuli, and clearance, antioxidant, and repair functions to damage containment. These functions can coexist without receiving equivalent metabolic support, and protective braking is distinct from generalized immunosuppression. Evidence differs across cells and experimental systems; metabolic regulation of inflammatory activation does not by itself establish metabolic control of NET-mediated injury in AP. The framework provides a basis for evaluating whether metabolic interventions can limit damaging activity while preserving protective functions, but it is not a validated clinical model. Pairing metabolic changes with specific cellular functions and subsequent injury is central to testing these relationships.

articles.titulo: The Aldosterone-Immune Axis in Primary Aldosteronism: Linking Adrenal Pathogenesis to Systemic Inflammation and Target-Organ Damage.
articles.autores: Zaidi NE, Azizan EA, Ali A
articles.resumo_original: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension and is increasingly recognised as a systemic disorder extending beyond haemodynamic dysregulation. Accumulating evidence suggests that chronic autonomous aldosterone excess promotes maladaptive immune activation, establishing an aldosterone-immune axis that may contribute to cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic injury independently of blood pressure elevation. In some patients, glucocorticoid co-secretion may further amplify tissue-specific mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) signalling. Human and experimental studies indicate that aldosterone modulates both innate and adaptive immunity. Patients with PA demonstrate altered monocyte transcriptional profiles, enhanced vascular inflammatory activity, and increased pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling in monocyte-derived macrophages compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension controls. Experimental models further show that sustained aldosterone exposure promotes macrophage M1 polarisation, dendritic cell activation, Th17 expansion, and regulatory T-cell suppression. These inflammatory changes are accompanied by oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, fibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix remodelling across cardiovascular and renal tissues. Emerging evidence is also consistent with a role for trained innate immunity, whereby prolonged aldosterone exposure may induce persistent epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of monocytes and macrophages. Whether such reprogramming persists after biochemical correction by adrenalectomy or MR antagonism in human PA has not yet been directly demonstrated and remains an important open question. If confirmed, these mechanisms may help explain the partial irreversibility of target-organ damage despite successful treatment. This review synthesises current evidence linking adrenal somatic pathogenesis to systemic immune dysregulation and target-organ injury in PA. We propose that PA should be viewed not solely as a hypertensive disorder, but as a chronic fibro-inflammatory endocrine disease with important implications for early diagnosis, risk stratification, and targeted therapy. Future prospective human studies are needed to confirm the mechanistic hierarchy proposed and to identify the immunological targets most amenable to therapeutic intervention.

articles.titulo: Glucocorticoid Receptor Alpha as an Integrative Regulator of Host Defense: A Systems-Level Review and Framework for Immune Regulation and Homeostatic Correction.
articles.autores: Meduri GU
articles.resumo_original: Current concepts recognize that effective host defense depends on coordinated interactions among innate and adaptive immunity, inflammatory signaling, immunometabolic regulation, and multiple complementary adaptive biological processes. However, far less attention has focused on the regulatory systems that integrate these diverse responses across the evolving phases of the host response. This Review proposes that glucocorticoid receptor alpha (GRα) functions as a systems-level integrative regulator that may contribute to the integration of immune signaling, antimicrobial competence, mitochondrial bioenergetics, inflammatory regulation, and other adaptive processes across partially overlapping adaptive phases of homeostatic correction. A central premise is that these phase-specific actions are shaped by dynamic changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription-factor interactions, providing a molecular basis for differential GRα regulation throughout the adaptive response. Rather than functioning solely as a transcriptional regulator of inflammation, GRα influences biological processes involved in pathogen sensing, NF-κB/AP-1 signaling, immunometabolic adaptation, innate and adaptive immune responses, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, lymphatic function, tissue repair, and the transition from early host defense to inflammatory resolution and restoration of physiological homeostasis. These integrated biological processes are organized within the proposed Priming, Modulatory, and Restorative phases of homeostatic correction. By synthesizing evidence across multiple physiological systems, this Review provides a biologically plausible model for understanding how GRα-associated regulatory mechanisms may contribute to immune effectiveness, disease tolerance, host-defense outcomes, and adaptive recovery during infection and critical illness. The proposed model generates testable hypotheses to guide future mechanistic investigation and the development of precision therapeutic strategies.

articles.titulo: From emergency myelopoiesis to trained immunity? Reframing post-stroke myeloid reprogramming along the brain-bone marrow axis.
articles.autores: Wei T, Wang Y
articles.resumo_original: Ischemic stroke rapidly mobilizes myeloid cells from anatomically distinct bone-marrow niches, while emerging evidence indicates that severe cerebral injury can also leave a durable imprint on hematopoiesis. These observations have encouraged the use of the term trained immunity in stroke biology, but acute myeloid expansion is not equivalent to innate immune memory. In this Mini review, we distinguish acute myeloid activation, myelopoietic responses consistent with emergency myelopoiesis, and central trained immunity involving hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). We use an operational four-feature framework-persistence, progenitor involvement, epigenetic or metabolic reprogramming, and functional recall-to grade the strength of current evidence. We consider a sequential transition from emergency myelopoiesis to trained immunity as one testable possibility rather than an established pathway, while allowing for parallel or independent mechanisms. The key unresolved questions are where durable memory is stored, when acute hematopoietic adaptation becomes stabilized, and which outputs are maladaptive versus reparative. Resolving these boundaries is essential before marrow-directed immunomodulation can be translated to patients with ischemic stroke.

articles.titulo: Obesity-driven inflammation and immune dysregulation in cancer development and progression.
articles.autores: Pandey P, Struder JF, Rezeli ET, Paules EM, Hursting SD, Coleman MF, Altwegg KA
articles.resumo_original: Obesity increases the risk and progression of at least 13 types of cancer. Although the epidemiologic links between excess adiposity and these cancers are well documented, the biological mechanisms linking obesity to carcinogenesis and tumor progression remain incompletely understood. White adipose tissue in obesity is a source of inflammatory and immunosuppressive signals that act systemically, driving metabolic, inflammatory, and immune dysfunction whose consequences differ across tumor types. As adipose tissue expands and adipocytes enlarge, the blood supply becomes inadequate, leading to hypoxia, fibrosis, lipolytic stress, macrophage recruitment, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These obesity-induced perturbations generate endocrine, cytokine, lipid, and metabolic signals that act systemically, within the tumor microenvironment (TME), and/or cell-intrinsically to activate oncogenic and tumor-promoting pathways. The same signals reshape innate and adaptive immunity, promoting tumor-permissive macrophage states and myeloid-derived suppressor cell expansion, while the effector arms weaken as antigen presentation, natural killer cell and T cell function all decline. This review synthesizes current evidence linking obesity-associated inflammation and immune dysregulation to cancer initiation, progression, and treatment responses across multiple obesity-related cancers. Emphasis is placed on adipose tissue inflammation, myeloid cell biology, T cell immunometabolism, endocrine-inflammatory crosstalk, and the relationship between obesity and immunotherapy. Finally, we discuss translational opportunities for preventing or intercepting obesity-related cancers, including weight loss achieved through lifestyle, surgical, or pharmacologic approaches, with an emphasis on GLP-1 receptor agonists given their substantial efficacy, rapid clinical uptake, and potential to reshape obesity-related cancer prevention and survivorship strategies. Defining the metabolic, immune, and inflammatory phenotypes that drive obesity-associated cancer risk and progression will be essential for developing more precise, mechanism-based strategies for prevention, treatment, and survivorship care.

articles.titulo: Metabolic stress and macrophage efferocytosis in osteoarthritis: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
articles.autores: Wu H, Yuan D, He R, Liu S
articles.resumo_original: Metabolic disturbances contribute to osteoarthritis through mechanisms that extend beyond increased mechanical loading, yet their effects on inflammatory resolution remain incompletely understood. Macrophage efferocytosis-the recognition, engulfment, and degradation of apoptotic cells-provides a potential link between metabolic stress and persistent synovitis. This Mini Review examines how obesity and hyperglycemia disrupt synovial macrophage clearance and evaluates the rationale for therapeutic restoration. Human observations and experimental osteoarthritis studies implicate reduced growth arrest-specific 6 signaling and hyperglycemia-associated CD11b lactylation in defective apoptotic-cell recognition and uptake. Complementary evidence from other inflammatory conditions identifies membrane trafficking, mitochondrial adaptation, and lysosomal cargo processing as additional determinants of clearance competence. Importantly, glycolysis and lactate have context-dependent effects: although lactylation can impair recognition, adaptive lactate signaling supports repeated engulfment and expansion of pro-resolving macrophages.
